title: SameSite Cookies
summary: The SameSite attribute on a cookie tells the browser whether to attach that cookie to requests that originate from another site, and it is the mechanism behind a large part of modern cross site request forgery defence. A value of Strict sends the cookie only on same site requests, Lax sends it on top level navigations that use safe methods such as a link click, and None sends it everywhere but only when the cookie is also marked Secure. In a real application it protects session cookies by stopping a page on another origin from silently causing an authenticated request, while still allowing a normal link from an email to land the user logged in. The mistake people make is to set None on a session cookie to fix a broken embed or payment redirect, which removes the defence entirely, or to assume the attribute replaces controls such as token checks and origin validation on state changing requests.

beginner.definition: SameSite is a setting on a cookie that controls when the browser sends it. A cookie marked Strict is sent only to the site that created it. A cookie marked Lax is sent when you follow a normal link to the site. None means the cookie is sent in more situations, and it needs extra protection.
beginner.whyItMatters: Browsers send cookies automatically with requests to your site. A harmful page can use that habit to make your logged in browser do things you did not intend. SameSite limits which requests carry the cookie. It reduces a common class of attack with a single setting. It is not enough on its own, but it removes an easy opening.
howItWorks: When a site sets a cookie, the server can add a SameSite instruction to it.
The browser records the site that created the cookie, called its site of origin.
On each later request the browser compares the request site with that recorded site.
With Strict, cross site requests lose the cookie, so a forged request arrives unauthenticated.
With Lax, the cookie is kept for safe top level navigation, such as clicking a link.
With None, the cookie is always sent, so the cookie must be Secure and other checks must exist.
beginner.example: Imagine a members only library where your card is checked at the door. A helpful rule lets the card work when you walk in through the main entrance. But the same rule should not let a stranger use your card through the back window. SameSite is that rule written on the card itself. It says where the card is accepted, so a request from the wrong place arrives without your name on it.
takeaways: SameSite decides whether a cookie travels with a request from another site.
Setting None on a session cookie removes a cross site request defence.
Combine SameSite with server side checks on requests that change data.

objectives: Explain what the SameSite cookie attribute controls.
Describe the difference between the Strict, Lax, and None values.
Explain how SameSite reduces cross site request forgery risk.
Recognise why the None value must be paired with the Secure attribute.
Identify situations where SameSite alone does not provide enough protection.
